- **Memory Footprint**: Significantly reduced compared to SVO when there are many identical subtrees [S2, unofficial].

The claim states that the memory footprint is significantly reduced compared to SVO when there are many identical subtrees. The evidence explicitly states that Sparse Voxel DAGs (an extension to SVO) work by 'merging identical nodes together' and are 'capable of decreasing the memory footprint further.' It further clarifies that this method works well for storing simple occlusion values (implying many identical subtrees/nodes) but becomes less effective for complex data like diffuse albedo because 'identical child nodes become rare.' Therefore, the evidence supports the condition that the reduction is effective (supported) when there are many identical subtrees.

The method extends the Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO) structure by allowing nodes to reference branches of other nodes, effectively creating a Directed Acyclic Graph rather than a strict tree [S1].

The claim states that the method extends the Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO) structure by allowing nodes to reference branches of other nodes, creating a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG). Source [S1] explicitly states that 'Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs) for voxel encoding build on the idea of octrees' and 'allow nodes to reference the branches of other nodes.' While the source uses the term 'octrees' generally rather than specifically 'Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO)', in the context of voxel encoding literature, DAGs are widely recognized as an extension of SVO structures to reduce redundancy. The core facts in the claim (extending octree/SVO, referencing branches, creating a DAG) are fully present and supported by the evidence.
